match.reason: The bank point teaches factorising techniques (common factor, grouping, difference of squares, perfect squares) but never states that factorising reverses expanding or that a factorised answer can be checked by expanding, so it is related rather than the same idea.

draft.title: Expanding and factorising as reverse processes
card: Expanding removes brackets by multiplying. For example, (x + 2)(x + 5) = x² + 5x + 2x + 10 = x² + 7x + 10.
Factorising goes the other way. It writes an expression as a product, so x² + 7x + 10 becomes (x + 2)(x + 5).
To check a factorised answer, expand it. If you get the original expression back, the factorising is right.
Example: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). Check: (x − 3)(x + 3) = x² + 3x − 3x − 9 = x² − 9. The middle terms cancel, so the check works.
draft.remember: Expand to check a factorised answer. If you get the start back, it is right.

a.q: Mia factorises x² − 25 as (x − 5)(x + 5). What is the best way to check her answer?
opts: Expand (x − 5)(x + 5) and compare it with x² − 25
Factorise x² − 25 a second time in the same way
Substitute x = 0 into the brackets only
Add 5 and −5 to see if they make 0
a.why: Expanding undoes factorising, so it should give x² − 25 back: x² + 5x − 5x − 25 = x² − 25. Factorising again repeats the same step and does not test it. One value of x alone could match by chance.

b.q: Liam factorises x² + 5x + 6 as (x + 1)(x + 6). Expanding his answer shows what?
opts: It gives x² + 7x + 6, so his factorising is wrong
It gives x² + 5x + 6, so his factorising is right
It gives x² + 6x + 7, so his factorising is wrong
It gives x² + 7x + 6, so his factorising is right
b.why: Expanding gives x² + 6x + x + 6 = x² + 7x + 6. This is not x² + 5x + 6, so the factorising is wrong. The constant term 6 matches, which is tempting, but the x term does not.
b.clue: Check the x term as well as the number.

a.best: Expand (x − 5)(x + 5) and compare it with x² − 25

b.best: It gives x² + 7x + 6, so his factorising is wrong
